context_block1_text: The archaeological site of Darró is not just a point on the map, but a true open book covering more than 1,000 years of history on the shores of the Mediterranean. Strategically located between the promontory of Sant Gervasi and the mouth of an ancient torrent, this space was for centuries a meeting point where various civilizations converged. From the first Iberian settlers to its transformation into a Roman villa and its subsequent Visigothic stage, Darró has been a crossroads where maritime trade and cultural exchange with Phoenicians, Greeks, and Carthaginians forged the identity of this territory long before the foundation of present-day Vilanova.
context_block2_text: Around the year 550 BC, the Iberian tribe of the Cosetani chose the hill of Sant Gervasi to establish their first settlement. This people, who possibly called the place Arró or Darró, became a key economic center in the Cosetania region. Over time, the settlement grew toward the plain, where an important industrial district developed. Excavations have revealed houses aligned along well-laid-out streets and, above all, intense metallurgical activity in the blacksmiths' quarter, as well as ceramic workshops where amphorae were manufactured to trade with the Carthaginians of the Pityusic Islands.
context_block3_text: The site is transformed with the arrival of Rome, becoming integrated into Mediterranean trade routes. With the arrival of Rome around 50 BC, the old Iberian settlement was replaced by a luxurious Roman villa linked to the territory of Tárraco. This agricultural and residential estate experienced its maximum splendor between the 1st and 4th centuries AD. The villa was divided into two clearly differentiated zones: the pars urbana, a stately residence with gardens, rich mosaics, and noble rooms decorated with Corinthian capitals, and the pars fructuaria, dedicated to the production of wine and oil and the storage of agricultural products. It was a time of great economic activity that left a monumental mark on the coastal landscape.
context_block4_text: Currently, the Darró Archaeological Site is a living heritage space that allows visitors to travel back in time right from the Ribes Roges promenade. Thanks to the excavations started in the 1950s and continued by the Local Architectural Heritage Service (SPAL) of the Barcelona Provincial Council, today visitors can explore the consolidated remains of the Iberian quarter and the Roman residence. The site has become an open-air museum where scientific research and restoration work hand in hand to preserve this legacy and offer visitors a direct window into the city's ancient past.
